Introduction
?

In previous lessons, we learned that the principal components of a standardized data matrix are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and that these eigenvectors appear as the columns of in the singular value decomposition We also learned that the variance along each principal component is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to use principal components to perform feature extraction — the process of projecting high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional subspace while preserving as much variance as possible.

To illustrate the idea, suppose a biologist has recorded the resting heart rate and breathing rate for four mammals of different sizes. Both measurements have been standardized, giving the data matrix

The biologist knows that body size strongly influences both heart rate and breathing rate — smaller animals tend to have faster rates for both. They want to extract a single "metabolic index" that captures this underlying factor. How should they proceed?

From the SVD the first principal component is

which points in the direction of maximum variance. To obtain a one-dimensional representation of the data, we project each row of onto this direction by computing

The result is a vector — one number per animal — that captures the variation in body size. The second animal, with the most negative standardized values (indicating a larger, slower-metabolizing animal), has the largest projected value.

The Projection Formula
?

More generally, suppose we have a standardized data matrix where each row is a data point and each column is a feature. To reduce the data from dimensions to dimensions, we project the data onto the first principal components. If is the matrix whose columns are the first principal components, the reduced data matrix is

Each row of is a -dimensional representation of the corresponding data point, expressed in terms of the principal component directions.

There is an equivalent way to compute using the SVD. Starting from we have

where is the matrix of the first columns of and is the diagonal matrix of the first singular values.

So, we can compute the reduced data either as or as

Watch out! The vector (the first column of ) is a direction — a unit vector in feature space pointing along maximum variance. By contrast, the product (equivalently, ) is the projected data — an vector giving each data point's coordinate along that direction. Some texts refer to this projected data as "the first principal component of the data" or as "scores," so the term "principal component" can mean either the direction or the projected values, depending on context.

Question 1
?

Suppose we have a dataset consisting of 4 datapoints with 2 features in the form of the 4×2 matrix X=[−0.331.18−0.49−0.881.490.48−0.66−0.77] where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is 0 and the standard deviation is 1). We are also given the SVD decomposition X=UΣVT where:

U=[0.290.8130.5050.021−0.469−0.2120.634−0.5780.676−0.540.4730.168−0.49−0.0610.3450.798]Σ=[2.065001.3160000]V=[0.709−0.7050.7050.709]

Which of the following matrices corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance?

  1. [0.7090.705]
  2. [−0.331.18−0.49−0.881.490.48−0.66−0.77]⋅[0.7090.705]
  3. [0.29−0.4690.676−0.49]⋅2.065
a
II only
b
I and II only
c
III only
d
I and III only
e
II and III only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance is the projection onto the first principal component.

Recall that the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix XTX.

Using the SVD and the fact that U is orthogonal (i.e., UTU=I), we get that

XTX=(UΣVT)T(UΣVT)=VΣTUTUΣVT=VΣTΣVT.

Now, since Σ is a diagonal matrix, and so is ΣTΣ, we know that the eigenvectors of XTX are the columns of V.

In particular, the first principal component is the eigenvector of XTX corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. And since Σ contains the corresponding singular values (square roots of the eigenvalues) in decreasing order, the first principal component is v1, the first column of V.

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

  • Option I represents v1, which is the first principal component. It represents a direction in feature space, not a version of the data. Notice that it is also dimensionally incorrect, since it is a 2×1 matrix instead of 4×1.

  • Option II corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance. Indeed, it represents X⋅v1, which is exactly the projection of X onto the first principal component.

  • Option III corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance. Notice that it represents u1⋅σ1, where u1 is the first column of U and σ1 is the first singular value. But this equals X⋅v1:

X⋅v1=UΣVT⋅v1=UΣ⋅[10]=U⋅[σ1000]=u1⋅σ1.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Choosing the Number of Components
?

In the previous section, we saw how to project data onto the first principal components. But how do we choose Keeping more components preserves more information, while keeping fewer gives a more compact representation at the cost of discarding some variation.

Recall that the variance along the th principal component is proportional to where is the th singular value. Therefore, the fraction of total variance preserved by keeping the first components is

While the amount of variance we need to preserve depends on the application, as a rule of thumb, we will choose the smallest that preserves at least of the variance. That is, we select such that

We are also given the SVD decomposition X=UΣVT where:

U=[−0.1860.2570.252−0.792−0.4560.3980.5930.30.45−0.4430.529−0.7080.123−0.057−0.447−0.0150.115−0.8870.015−0.446−0.725−0.2590.2080.408−0.443]Σ=[2.87800002.15200001.63600000.6520000]V=[−0.6−0.4190.045−0.680.38−0.5250.7610.040.6540.205−0.148−0.7130.262−0.712−0.630.166]

Correct
EXPLANATION

In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible.

We should pick components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are σ1=2.878,σ2=2.152,σ3=1.636,σ4=0.652.

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is σ12∑i=14σi2=2.87822.8782+2.1522+1.6362+0.6522≈51.7%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is ∑i=12σi2∑i=14σi2=2.8782+2.15222.8782+2.1522+1.6362+0.6522≈80.6%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first three principal components is ∑i=13σi2∑i=14σi2=2.8782+2.1522+1.63622.8782+2.1522+1.6362+0.6522≈97.3%.

Thus, we obtain that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 51.7% of the variance,

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 80.6% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 3 dimensions would preserve 97.3% of the variance.

Therefore, we should reduce the dataset to 3 dimensions, since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 90% of the variance.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first three principal components is ∑i=13σi2∑i=14σi2=3.0412+1.9672+1.67123.0412+1.9672+1.6712+0.2682≈99.6%.

Thus, we obtain that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 57.9% of the variance,

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 82.1% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 3 dimensions would preserve 99.6% of the variance.

Therefore, we should reduce the dataset to 3 dimensions, since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 90% of the variance.

The Feature Extraction Pipeline
?

We can now summarize the complete pipeline for using PCA to extract features from a dataset.

  1. Standardize the data. Subtract the mean of each feature and divide by its standard deviation. This ensures that all features contribute equally to the analysis, regardless of their original units or scales.

  2. Compute the SVD. Find the singular value decomposition The columns of are the principal components, and the diagonal entries of are the singular values.

  3. Choose the number of components. Using the singular values, compute the cumulative variance for each possible choice of and select the smallest that preserves at least of the variance.

  4. Project the data. Compute the reduced data matrix where consists of the first columns of

To interpret results in terms of the original features or to apply the same transformation to new data, we must keep track of the means and standard deviations used in Step 1.
